newsitem.title: RWANDA: Aid workers in Rwanda may pull out after killings.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers in Rwanda may pull out after killings.

text.p: International aid workers hold crisis talks on Monday on whether to suspend relief operations in some parts of Rwanda after the murder of three Spaniards at the weekend.

"The meeting will decide whether to formally suspend humanitarian work in parts of Rwanda on security grounds," a senior aid official in Kigali told Reuters. "The government will also be represented."
Rwandan Hutu militiamen shot dead three Spanish aid workers and three soldiers and seriously wounded an American in an overnight attack in the northwestern town of Ruhengeri.
"These people were executed. Clearly these attacks were aimed at aid workers and expatriates generally," United Nations Human Rights Operation director Javier Zuniga told Reuters.

A U.S. diplomat said the attackers stormed into the house and demanded the Spaniards' passports. They were then disturbed by the noise of gunfire outside the house and reacted by shooting the three at close range.

The Spaniards, shot through the head, were attached to the Spanish charity Medicos del Mundo (Doctors of the World). It named them as Dr Manuel Madrazo, 42, nurse Maria Flors Sirera, 33, and Luis Valtuena, 30, a photographer working as an administrator.

The American, Nitin Madhav, 28, from the Pittsburgh area of Pennyslvania, was shot in the leg as he dived behind a table. He was treated in Ruhengeri hospital, where his leg was amputated, and later flown to Kigali and evacuated for further treatment.
In Paris, the parent group Medecins du Monde announced that it was suspending all activities in Rwanda pending further information about the killings.

The Spanish Foreign Ministry said it was advising its nationals to leave Rwanda. Most expatriates in the Ruhengeri area left for Kigali where the United Nations, international relief groups and the government will hold the crisis meeting.
"Most of the expatriates in Ruhengeri have already reached Kigali. The mood is very sombre," a Western diplomat said.
A senior Rwandan military officer told Reuters: "These attacks are deliberately mounted to scare away expatriates."
"U.N. people have been told to stay put and not go out. And as soon as we have talked to the army we will be discussing whether or not to suspend operations," a U.N. official said.

Another U.N. official said: "The fighting appeared to have started in the slum areas of town among returnees who have come back from Zaire. There were two other incidents during the night during which a grenade was thrown into an aid worker's house."

The attack was the latest in a series involving foreign workers in the area near the border with Zaire. U.N. officials warned on Saturday that escalating violence could force the suspension of humanitarian operations in some areas.

"I am surprised at the violence. I'd rather not put people in danger and if this violence continues then I have no option but to suspend operations in some areas," Omar Bakhet, the United Nations' Rwanda coordinator, told Reuters.

Hardline Hutu militiamen, troops and mobs killed an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994. Many of the militiamen fled to neighbouring countries after Tutsi rebels seized power.

Two U.N. vehicles were attacked with gunfire and hand grenades at Giciyi, in southern Gisenyi prefecture, last Monday and Wednesday and two expatriate staff were beaten by Hutu militia, according to U.N. officials.
Grenades were thrown at a road construction lorry run by a Chinese company last Tuesday and 12 Rwandans were killed by militiamen outside Giciyi.
